citations.claim_context: This division of labour can extend both knowledge coverage and effective context capacity. Different agents may use complementary prompts, tools, or evidence sources, so diversity is beneficial when it contributes independent evidence rather than duplicated model calls. Likewise, segmenting a large document across agents can support broader coverage than a single context, as explored by LongAgent and Chain-of-Agents \citep{zhao2024longagent,zhang2024chain_agents}. These gains are conditional: intermediate results must still be communicated and synthesized, and aggregation loss, communication cost, and the final synthesis context can become new bottlenecks.

citations.claim_context: Knowledge-intensive QA can assign planning, retrieval, generation, and verification to a staged workflow. Representative implementations include LONGAGENT \citep{zhao2024longagent}, which coordinates a leader with document-reading members; Chain-of-Agents \citep{zhang2024chain_agents}, which propagates information across context segments before synthesis; and CoCoA-zero \citep{jiang2026cocoa}, which coordinates parametric and retrieved knowledge using three agents at inference time. CoCoA subsequently distils that collaboration into a single model. These role-I systems differ in their communication and aggregation mechanisms, but each places subtask sequencing or synthesis under explicit control. By contrast, HuggingGPT \citep{shen2024hugginggpt} uses a controller to invoke specialised models and tools.

This mechanism cannot be simplified to a "simple-flat/complex- hierarchical" rule. MDAgents \citep{kim2024mdagents} routes medical queries to solo, multidisciplinary-team, or integrated-care-team pathways according to complexity under a moderator. This supports adaptive collaboration, but a persistent moderator means that mode switching alone is insufficient to prove hybrid authority. State management and performance still require evaluation.

citations.claim_context: For complex QA tasks, LLMs often cannot answer in a single step. Hierarchical task decomposition reduces difficulty by breaking complex queries into sub-tasks that can be processed in parallel or sequentially. Representative methods include Least-to-Most Prompting \citep{zhou2023least_to_most} and Decomposed Prompting \citep{khot2023decomposed_prompting}, which allow a model to solve simpler sub-problems first and then exploit their answers to resolve the ultimate target. Plan-and-Solve \citep{wang2023plan_and_solve} provides another example by explicitly separating planning from solving and reducing missing-step errors on the evaluated reasoning tasks. Formally, given a complex query $Q$, a decomposition function $\mathcal{D}$ maps it to an ordered sequence of sub-tasks: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{D}(Q) &\to \{q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_m\}, \\ \operatorname{Answer}(Q) &= \mathcal{F}\!\left(\operatorname{Sol}(q_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Sol}(q_m)\right) \end{aligned} \label{eq:decompose} \end{equation} where $\operatorname{Sol}(q_i)$ is a sub-agent's solution to sub-task $q_i$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is an aggregation function (e.g., voting, concatenation, or re-generation).

citations.claim_context: For complex QA tasks, LLMs often cannot answer in a single step. Hierarchical task decomposition reduces difficulty by breaking complex queries into sub-tasks that can be processed in parallel or sequentially. Representative methods include Least-to-Most Prompting \citep{zhou2023least_to_most} and Decomposed Prompting \citep{khot2023decomposed_prompting}, which allow a model to solve simpler sub-problems first and then exploit their answers to resolve the ultimate target. Plan-and-Solve \citep{wang2023plan_and_solve} provides another example by explicitly separating planning from solving and reducing missing-step errors on the evaluated reasoning tasks. Formally, given a complex query $Q$, a decomposition function $\mathcal{D}$ maps it to an ordered sequence of sub-tasks: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{D}(Q) &\to \{q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_m\}, \\ \operatorname{Answer}(Q) &= \mathcal{F}\!\left(\operatorname{Sol}(q_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Sol}(q_m)\right) \end{aligned} \label{eq:decompose} \end{equation} where $\operatorname{Sol}(q_i)$ is a sub-agent's solution to sub-task $q_i$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is an aggregation function (e.g., voting, concatenation, or re-generation).

citations.claim_context: Static assignment can be inefficient when task difficulty and agent capabilities vary across queries. For example, DSPy \citep{khattab2024dspy} addresses a related but narrower problem: it represents language-model pipelines as declarative modules and compiles their prompts and demonstrations against a task metric. It should therefore be regarded as a pipeline-optimization toolkit rather than evidence supporting runtime multi-agent load balancing. Dynamic agent recruitment, routing, and early stopping remain distinct orchestration decisions that require task-specific evaluation.

citations.claim_context: Decomposition, assignment, and orchestration solve related but distinct problems. Decomposition determines which sub-questions must be answered and how they depend on one another; assignment matches those sub-questions to agents; orchestration determines their execution order and whether the workflow should adapt at runtime. Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting, and Plan-and-Solve primarily inform the first decision, whereas role profiles in MetaGPT and AgentVerse address the second \citep{zhou2023least_to_most,khot2023decomposed_prompting, wang2023plan_and_solve,hong2024metagpt,chen2024agentverse}. A fixed sequence is adequate when dependencies and agent capabilities are known in advance; dynamic routing may be more suitable when query difficulty or available expertise varies, but it adds scheduling overhead and failure points. In either case, decomposition errors can propagate: omitted sub-questions leave gaps in the final answer, while unnecessary decomposition creates redundant calls and aggregation work. Pipeline-optimization tools such as DSPy can improve task-metric performance of language-model modules, but should not be treated as evidence that runtime recruitment or load balancing is effective \citep{khattab2024dspy}. Evaluation should distinguish decomposition quality, assignment fit, and orchestration efficiency rather than attributing an end-to-end gain to a single mechanism.

citations.claim_context: Decomposition, assignment, and orchestration solve related but distinct problems. Decomposition determines which sub-questions must be answered and how they depend on one another; assignment matches those sub-questions to agents; orchestration determines their execution order and whether the workflow should adapt at runtime. Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting, and Plan-and-Solve primarily inform the first decision, whereas role profiles in MetaGPT and AgentVerse address the second \citep{zhou2023least_to_most,khot2023decomposed_prompting, wang2023plan_and_solve,hong2024metagpt,chen2024agentverse}. A fixed sequence is adequate when dependencies and agent capabilities are known in advance; dynamic routing may be more suitable when query difficulty or available expertise varies, but it adds scheduling overhead and failure points. In either case, decomposition errors can propagate: omitted sub-questions leave gaps in the final answer, while unnecessary decomposition creates redundant calls and aggregation work. Pipeline-optimization tools such as DSPy can improve task-metric performance of language-model modules, but should not be treated as evidence that runtime recruitment or load balancing is effective \citep{khattab2024dspy}. Evaluation should distinguish decomposition quality, assignment fit, and orchestration efficiency rather than attributing an end-to-end gain to a single mechanism.

citations.claim_context: Long-term memory can retain historical experiences and domain knowledge in external stores \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents. As one illustrative multi-agent implementation, a retrieval agent can select the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ using cosine similarity: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)} {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad \hat{\mathcal{D}} = \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) \label{eq:rag} \end{equation} where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has evolved from passive retrieval to active variants. Self-RAG \citep{asai2024selfrag} uses reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique generated passages, while FLARE \citep{jiang2023active_rag} triggers retrieval when predicted upcoming text contains low-confidence tokens and then regenerates that text. These controls can inform retrieval components in a multi-agent workflow.

stage2_prior_context.original_sentence: Long-term memory can retain historical experiences and domain knowledge in external stores \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}.
stage2_prior_context.context: Long-term memory can retain historical experiences and domain knowledge in external stores \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents. As one illustrative multi-agent implementation, a retrieval agent can select the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ using cosine similarity: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)} {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad \hat{\mathcal{D}} = \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) \label{eq:rag} \end{equation} where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has evolved from passive retrieval to active variants. Self-RAG \citep{asai2024selfrag} uses reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique generated passages, while FLARE \citep{jiang2023active_rag} triggers retrieval when predicted upcoming text contains low-confidence tokens and then regenerates that text. These controls can inform retrieval components in a multi-agent workflow.

citations.claim_context: Short-term and long-term memory address different temporal scopes. Working memory supports continuity within the current interaction and must prioritise information under a limited context budget; long-term memory extends access beyond that context, but depends on retrieval relevance and the quality and currency of stored experiences or documents. MemGPT illustrates session-context management, whereas RAG and its retrieval variants provide access to information outside the active context \citep{packer2023memgpt,lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey,asai2024selfrag, jiang2023active_rag}. A system should therefore specify what is retained, for how long, and under what conditions memories are updated or discarded.

stage2_prior_context.original_sentence: MemGPT illustrates session-context management, whereas RAG and its retrieval variants provide access to information outside the active context \citep{packer2023memgpt,lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey,asai2024selfrag, jiang2023active_rag}.
stage2_prior_context.context: Short-term and long-term memory address different temporal scopes. Working memory supports continuity within the current interaction and must prioritise information under a limited context budget; long-term memory extends access beyond that context, but depends on retrieval relevance and the quality and currency of stored experiences or documents. MemGPT illustrates session-context management, whereas RAG and its retrieval variants provide access to information outside the active context \citep{packer2023memgpt,lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey,asai2024selfrag, jiang2023active_rag}. A system should therefore specify what is retained, for how long, and under what conditions memories are updated or discarded.

citations.claim_context: For ultra-long-text QA, the attention mechanism of conventional Transformers faces severe computational bottlenecks. Chain-of-Agents \citep{zhang2024chain_agents} distributes evidence processing across worker agents, while Tree of Thoughts \citep{yao2023tree_of_thoughts} and Graph of Thoughts \citep{besta2024graph_of_thoughts} organise intermediate reasoning states as search structures. In Chain-of-Agents, worker agents process successive text chunks and pass forward condensed evidence before a manager produces the answer. LONGAGENT \citep{zhao2024longagent} uses a different leader--member design in which a leader coordinates member agents over long-document segments. Tree- and graph-structured reasoning provide related search topologies, but are not necessarily multi-agent systems in their original formulations.

LONGAGENT \citep{zhao2024longagent} uses a different leader--member design in which a leader coordinates member agents over long-document segments. Tree- and graph-structured reasoning provide related search topologies, but are not necessarily multi-agent systems in their original formulations.

citations.claim_context: These techniques seek reliability through different mechanisms. Self-consistency and debate broaden the set of candidate reasoning paths; Chain-of-Agents distributes evidence processing across long inputs; reflection and critique revisit a provisional answer to identify and repair errors \citep{wang2023self_consistency,du2024multiagent_debate, zhang2024chain_agents,shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023self_refine, dhuliawala2023chain_of_verification}. They are not interchangeable: sampling more paths helps only when those paths provide meaningful diversity, sequential evidence transfer can lose information, and a critic may share the generator's blind spots. Combining mechanisms is possible, but each extra pass adds inference cost and requires an aggregation or stopping rule. The appropriate choice therefore depends on the dominant failure mode: ambiguity among plausible answers, limited capacity to process long evidence, or the need to audit a provisional response. Reliability should be evaluated against these failure modes rather than inferred from the number of agents or reasoning rounds.

citations.claim_context: The orchestration layer determines how agents are defined, assigned work, and coordinated during execution. Figure~\ref{fig:platform_resource_map} illustrates this layer with AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT \citep{wu2024autogen,crewai2023,hong2024metagpt}. Across the wider set of resources, some frameworks encode collaboration through predefined roles and procedures: for example, CAMEL uses role-conditioned dialogue, while ChatDev and MetaGPT organize work through staged, role-based processes \citep{li2023camel,qian2023chatdev,hong2024metagpt}. Other frameworks expose more control flow to developers: AutoGen supports configurable conversations, LangGraph represents workflows as state graphs, and AgentVerse provides a phased collaboration process \citep{wu2024autogen,duan2024langgraph_crewai, chen2024agentverse}. GPTSwarm explores optimization of agent connections. DSPy, by contrast, focuses on metric-driven optimization of language-model pipelines and is therefore an adjacent toolkit, not a like-for-like multi-agent framework \citep{zhuge2024gptswarm,khattab2024dspy}.

Figure~\ref{fig:platform_resource_map} illustrates this layer with AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT \citep{wu2024autogen,crewai2023,hong2024metagpt}. Across the wider set of resources, some frameworks encode collaboration through predefined roles and procedures: for example, CAMEL uses role-conditioned dialogue, while ChatDev and MetaGPT organize work through staged, role-based processes \citep{li2023camel,qian2023chatdev,hong2024metagpt}. Other frameworks expose more control flow to developers: AutoGen supports configurable conversations, LangGraph represents workflows as state graphs, and AgentVerse provides a phased collaboration process \citep{wu2024autogen,duan2024langgraph_crewai, chen2024agentverse}. GPTSwarm explores optimization of agent connections. DSPy, by contrast, focuses on metric-driven optimization of language-model pipelines and is therefore an adjacent toolkit, not a like-for-like multi-agent framework \citep{zhuge2024gptswarm,khattab2024dspy}.

citations.claim_context: The human-in-the-loop pattern in Section~3.1 and the evidence and reasoning mechanisms in Section~4 make review possible, but a breakpoint alone does not provide accountable oversight. Reviewers need to inspect relevant sources, agent contributions, uncertainty, and state changes, and they need authority appropriate to the decision. Medical and legal QA provide application contexts for these proposed oversight requirements \citep{tang2024medagents,cui2023chatlaw}. Frameworks support configurable interaction and workflow control \citep{duan2024langgraph_crewai, langgraph2024interrupt}. Their use still requires designers to specify when intervention is useful, what can be revised, and how the intervention affects subsequent reasoning. Oversight that is too late cannot correct upstream retrieval or decomposition errors, while review at every stage may impose excessive latency and workload.

citations.claim_context:
This division of labour can extend both knowledge coverage and effective
context capacity. Different agents may use complementary prompts, tools, or
evidence sources, so diversity is beneficial when it contributes independent
evidence rather than duplicated model calls. Likewise, segmenting a large
document across agents can support broader coverage than a single context,
as explored by LongAgent and Chain-of-Agents
\citep{zhao2024longagent,zhang2024chain_agents}. These gains are conditional:
intermediate results must still be communicated and synthesized, and
aggregation loss, communication cost, and the final synthesis context can
become new bottlenecks.

citations.claim_context:
Knowledge-intensive QA can assign planning, retrieval, generation, and
verification to a staged workflow. Representative implementations include
LONGAGENT \citep{zhao2024longagent}, which coordinates a leader with
document-reading members; Chain-of-Agents \citep{zhang2024chain_agents},
which propagates information across context segments before synthesis; and
CoCoA \citep{jiang2026cocoa}, which coordinates parametric and retrieved
knowledge for QA. These role-I systems differ in their communication
and aggregation mechanisms, but each places subtask sequencing or synthesis
under explicit control. By contrast, HuggingGPT \citep{shen2024hugginggpt}
uses a controller to invoke specialised models and tools.

citations.claim_context:
For complex QA tasks, LLMs often cannot answer in a single step.
Hierarchical task decomposition reduces difficulty by breaking complex queries
into sub-tasks that can be processed in parallel or sequentially.
Representative methods include Least-to-Most Prompting
\citep{zhou2023least_to_most} and Decomposed Prompting
\citep{khot2023decomposed_prompting}, which allow a model to solve simpler
sub-problems first and then exploit their answers to resolve the ultimate
target. Plan-and-Solve \citep{wang2023plan_and_solve} provides another example
by explicitly separating
the planning and solving phases, substantially improving decomposition
reliability.
Formally, given a complex query $Q$, a decomposition function $\mathcal{D}$
maps it to an ordered sequence of sub-tasks:
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{D}(Q) &\to \{q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_m\}, \\
    \operatorname{Answer}(Q) &=
    \mathcal{F}\!\left(\operatorname{Sol}(q_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Sol}(q_m)\right)
  \end{aligned}
  \label{eq:decompose}
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{Sol}(q_i)$ is a sub-agent's solution to sub-task $q_i$
and $\mathcal{F}$ is an aggregation function (e.g., voting, concatenation, or
re-generation).

citations.claim_context:
Decomposition, assignment, and orchestration
solve related but distinct problems. Decomposition determines which
sub-questions must be answered and how they depend on one another; assignment
matches those sub-questions to agents; orchestration determines their
execution order and whether the workflow should adapt at runtime.
Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting, and Plan-and-Solve primarily inform the
first decision, whereas role profiles in MetaGPT and AgentVerse address the
second \citep{zhou2023least_to_most,khot2023decomposed_prompting,
wang2023plan_and_solve,hong2024metagpt,chen2024agentverse}. A fixed sequence
is adequate when dependencies and agent capabilities are known in advance;
dynamic routing may be more suitable when query difficulty or available
expertise varies, but it adds scheduling overhead and failure points. In
either case, decomposition errors can propagate: omitted sub-questions leave
gaps in the final answer, while unnecessary decomposition creates redundant
calls and aggregation work. Pipeline-optimization tools such as DSPy can
improve task-metric performance of language-model modules, but should not be
treated as evidence that runtime recruitment or load balancing is effective
\citep{khattab2024dspy}. Evaluation should distinguish decomposition quality,
assignment fit, and orchestration efficiency rather than attributing an
end-to-end gain to a single mechanism.

citations.claim_context:
Long-term memory typically relies on vector databases to store vast
historical experiences and external domain knowledge
\citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. A representative access mechanism is
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey},
through which multi-agent QA systems access long-term memory. A retrieval
agent selects the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$
using cosine similarity:
\begin{equation}
  \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) =
  \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)}
       {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad
  \hat{\mathcal{D}} =
  \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i)
  \label{eq:rag}
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and
$\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has
evolved from early passive Naive RAG to active variants. For example, Self-RAG
\citep{asai2024selfrag} and proactive retrieval (FLARE)
\citep{jiang2023active_rag} allow specialised retrieval agents to autonomously
determine when to retrieve, evaluate retrieval quality, and pass refined
knowledge to the generation agent.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey},
through which multi-agent QA systems access long-term memory. A retrieval
agent selects the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$
using cosine similarity:
\begin{equation}
  \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) =
  \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)}
       {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad
  \hat{\mathcal{D}} =
  \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i)
  \label{eq:rag}
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and
$\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has
evolved from early passive Naive RAG to active variants. For example, Self-RAG
\citep{asai2024selfrag} and proactive retrieval (FLARE)
\citep{jiang2023active_rag} allow specialised retrieval agents to autonomously
determine when to retrieve, evaluate retrieval quality, and pass refined
knowledge to the generation agent.

Short-term and long-term memory address
different temporal scopes. Working memory supports continuity within the
current interaction and must prioritise information under a limited context
budget; long-term memory extends access beyond that context, but depends on
retrieval relevance and the quality and currency of stored experiences or
documents. MemGPT illustrates session-context management, whereas RAG and its
retrieval variants provide access to information outside the active context
\citep{packer2023memgpt,lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey,asai2024selfrag,
jiang2023active_rag}. A system should therefore specify what is retained, for
how long, and under what conditions memories are updated or discarded.

For ultra-long-text QA, the attention mechanism of conventional
Transformers faces severe computational bottlenecks.
Representative search topologies include Chain-of-Agents
\citep{zhang2024chain_agents}, Tree of Thoughts
\citep{yao2023tree_of_thoughts}, and Graph of Thoughts
\citep{besta2024graph_of_thoughts}; these distribute reasoning across multiple
serially or graph-connected agents.
In Chain-of-Agents, worker agents process successive text chunks and pass
forward condensed evidence before a manager produces the answer. LONGAGENT
\citep{zhao2024longagent} uses a different leader--member design in which a
leader coordinates member agents over long-document segments. Tree- and
graph-structured reasoning provide related search topologies, but are not
necessarily multi-agent systems in their original formulations.

citations.claim_context:
These techniques seek reliability through
different mechanisms. Self-consistency and debate broaden the set of candidate
reasoning paths; Chain-of-Agents distributes evidence processing across long
inputs; reflection and critique revisit a provisional answer to identify and
repair errors \citep{wang2023self_consistency,du2024multiagent_debate,
zhang2024chain_agents,shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023self_refine,
dhuliawala2023chain_of_verification}. They are not interchangeable: sampling
more paths helps only when those paths provide meaningful diversity,
sequential evidence transfer can lose information, and a critic may share the
generator's blind spots. Combining mechanisms is possible, but each extra
pass adds inference cost and requires an aggregation or stopping rule. The
appropriate choice therefore depends on the dominant failure mode: ambiguity
among plausible answers, limited capacity to process long evidence, or the
need to audit a provisional response. Reliability should be evaluated against
these failure modes rather than inferred from the number of agents or
reasoning rounds.

citations.claim_context:
The orchestration layer determines how agents are defined, assigned work, and
coordinated during execution. Figure~\ref{fig:platform_resource_map}
illustrates this layer with AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT
\citep{wu2024autogen,crewai2023,hong2024metagpt}. Across the wider set of
resources, some frameworks encode collaboration through predefined roles and
procedures: for example, CAMEL uses role-conditioned dialogue, while ChatDev
and MetaGPT organize work through staged, role-based processes
\citep{li2023camel,qian2023chatdev,hong2024metagpt}. Other frameworks expose
more control flow to developers: AutoGen supports configurable conversations,
LangGraph represents workflows as state graphs, and AgentVerse provides a
phased collaboration process \citep{wu2024autogen,duan2024langgraph_crewai,

citations.claim_context:
The human-in-the-loop pattern in Section~3.1 and the evidence and reasoning
mechanisms in Section~4 make review possible, but a breakpoint alone does not
provide accountable oversight. Reviewers need to inspect relevant sources,
agent contributions, uncertainty, and state changes, and they need authority
appropriate to the decision. Medical and legal QA illustrate these demands
\citep{tang2024medagents,cui2023chatlaw}. Yet many workflows provide only a
textual correction or final approval \citep{duan2024langgraph_crewai,
langgraph2024}, without specifying when intervention is useful, what can be
revised, or how the intervention affects subsequent reasoning. Oversight that
is too late cannot correct upstream retrieval or decomposition errors, while
review at every stage may impose excessive latency and workload.

provide accountable oversight. Reviewers need to inspect relevant sources,
agent contributions, uncertainty, and state changes, and they need authority
appropriate to the decision. Medical and legal QA illustrate these demands
\citep{tang2024medagents,cui2023chatlaw}. Yet many workflows provide only a
textual correction or final approval \citep{duan2024langgraph_crewai,
langgraph2024}, without specifying when intervention is useful, what can be
revised, or how the intervention affects subsequent reasoning. Oversight that
is too late cannot correct upstream retrieval or decomposition errors, while
review at every stage may impose excessive latency and workload.

communication pattern, and stopping conditions, rather than treating these as
independent configuration choices. A controller could estimate task

results likewise indicate that the value of more agents depends on task and
coordination design \citep{qian2024scaling_multiagent}.

citations.claim_context:
At the group level, systems could learn which agents are reliable for
particular question types, which combinations contribute complementary
evidence, and which interaction patterns repeat errors. These histories could
inform routing, speaking order, voting weights, and stopping rules, extending
individual memory towards learned team coordination
\citep{park2023generative_agents,chen2024agentverse}. Longitudinal studies
should compare individual updating, team-policy updating, and their
combination on sequential tasks with changing knowledge. They should measure
adaptation speed, retention, long-term accuracy, and cost, while testing for
error propagation, collective bias, catastrophic forgetting, privacy leakage,
and unstable shifts in agent authority.
